subject: religious-studies

moments.title: Aquinas develops natural law
moments.body: Aquinas's natural law: eternal law (God's reason) is reflected in natural law (the law of human nature) and codified by divine law (revelation) and human law (positive law). Primary precepts: preserve life, reproduce, educate young, live in society, know God.
moments.takeaway: Natural law is a Catholic synthesis of Aristotelian teleology and biblical theology. The Aristotelian view that things have natures and purposes (teloi) underpins the moral conclusions.

moments.title: Natural law in international thought
moments.body: Spanish School (Suarez), then Protestant thinkers (Grotius's 'On the Law of War and Peace', 1625), develop natural law into the basis of international law and human rights theory. The 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man draws on natural-law assumptions.
moments.takeaway: Natural law was a major intellectual current of the 17th-18th centuries before being eclipsed by positivism and historicism in the 19th.

moments.title: Humanae Vitae and the contemporary debate
moments.body: 1968: Humanae Vitae's prohibition of artificial contraception is grounded in natural-law reasoning about the unitive and procreative aspects of sexual intercourse. Many lay Catholics and some theologians dissent. The natural-law framework is increasingly contested — and increasingly defended by 'new natural law' theorists (Finnis, Grisez, George).
moments.takeaway: Natural law continues to shape Catholic positions on contraception, abortion, euthanasia, marriage. New natural law theorists (John Finnis) defend it without the Aristotelian-Thomist metaphysics.

now.title: Natural law debated
now.body: Natural law is taught in every Catholic seminary. Outside Catholic moral theology, it is one option among many. Modern human rights discourse owes natural-law inheritance even when not acknowledged. Critics (Hume on is-ought, modern Darwinism on natures) have produced powerful objections.
now.open_questions: Does nature have purposes? The Aristotelian view that it does has been undermined by Darwinian biology in many readings. New natural lawyers (Finnis) defend the framework without Aristotelian biology by appeal to basic human goods.

reflection: Natural law is one of the longest-running ethical frameworks in Western thought. Its modern Catholic form is doctrinally fixed; its philosophical defenders continue to develop the framework; its critics are many. Few ethical traditions have lasted longer or generated more debate.
